title: Chesterton's fairyland
hookLine: Chesterton, in Orthodoxy (1908), argues life is a strange gift like a fairy tale

cards: Why is grass green? A small child asks, and the grown-up has an answer ready. Then the child asks why again, and again, until the grown-up runs out and says: it just is.
The English writer G. K. Chesterton thought that last answer deserved a much longer look.
In his book Orthodoxy there's a chapter called The Ethics of Elfland, and it starts in the nursery, with the fairy tales of his childhood.
Those stories, he says, taught him something about the real world that grown-up books had missed.

teach.b: In fairyland, nobody pretends a golden apple had to be golden.

teach.h: A LAW, OR A KIND OF MAGIC?
teach.b: It's magic: someone chose it. Chesterton turns that around on the world outside the window.

We call it a law that apples fall and leaves are green, and the word law makes it sound necessary, as if it couldn't have been any other way. But we don't actually know why it's this way and not another.
A world where grass happens to be green is a world someone might have chosen. Then he goes a step further. We tend to think repetition means something is dead, like a machine.
A laughing child says "Do it again!" and means it every single time.
Perhaps, he says, God makes each daisy separately and has never grown tired of making them, with the strength of a child who wants the same game over and over.

Jesus pointed somewhere nearby: "Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." And the psalmist, looking out at creation, doesn't explain it at all.
He marvels: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all." Chesterton's point isn't that the world is a fable.
It's that the world is stranger than a fable, and that being alive at all is a gift nobody earned.

teach.h: A GIFT WANTS SOMEONE TO THANK
teach.b: And a gift, he says, leaves you wanting someone to thank.

how: Christians who love Chesterton often read Orthodoxy as a book of gratitude and wonder rather than argument alone; churches also give thanks for creation in their prayers, and some Christians say grace before meals.

o: the plain world, as strange and chosen as a fairy tale
the idea that faith is a pleasant story for children
a land of make-believe to escape the real world

games.q: the world is strange — tap the pairs.
p: the chapter that starts in the nursery
a child's delight in the same game

s: Chesterton said the world is just a fable
he said it's stranger than a fable, and a gift nobody earned.
Chesterton suggested repetition might be a sign of life, not of deadness
like a child who says "do it again!" — perhaps God never tires of making each daisy.
Jesus spoke of becoming as little children
Matthew 18:3: "except ye be converted, and become as little children."

games.q: a small child keeps asking why grass is green. you run out of answers. what would Chesterton say?
o: it's a law; there's nothing more to say.
it might have been otherwise: someone chose it, and that's a wonder.
games.why: Chesterton said the word law hides the surprise. a world where grass happens to be green is a world someone might have chosen.

practice: Pick one plain thing within reach, a spoon, a key, a slice of bread, and look at it as if you'd stepped into a story and this was the first one you'd ever seen: why this color, this shape, why here at all?
Don't answer; let it be strange for a while. If you pray, you can borrow the psalmist's line: O Lord, how manifold are thy works.

wordCard.voice: Chesterton's fairyland. G. K. Chesterton's idea that the ordinary world is as strange and chosen as a fairy tale, and calls for thanks.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew 18:3: little children — "become as little children."
